title: Pizza dough
equipment: Mixer, flex-edge beater, dough hook, scales, covered bowl and pizza tray
time: 1–2 hours, including rise and baking
intro: An oil-rich tray pizza for a domestic oven—not the lean, high-heat Neapolitan dough from Ninety Seconds.
steps: Check your exact model’s batch limit. Keep dough-hook kneading at speed 2. Count preliminary heavy mixing toward a maximum 5-minute heavy-mixing run, then rest the mixer 20 minutes before continuing, or follow a stricter model manual. Stop immediately if the mixer strains; hand-finish rather than increasing speed.
Fit the flex-edge beater in the 4.7 L bowl. Combine dry ingredients at speed 2 for 15 seconds. Add water and oil at speed 2; mix 30–60 seconds until shaggy and joined.
Stop, fit hook. Knead at speed 2, 2–3 minutes until smoother, elastic and slightly tacky. Stop earlier if already developed; do not chase a dry dough.
Oil bowl, cover; prove about 30–60 minutes until doubled (source's 15–30 minutes may be optimistic in a cool room).

Gently deflate by hand, stretch/roll to tray; rest 10 minutes if it springs back. Add modest toppings. Bake 230°C conventional / 210°C fan, about 15–20 minutes, until crust is golden and base crisp and cooked. Cool 2 minutes before slicing.
cue: Golden crust with a crisp, cooked base.
troubleshoot: no rise: check yeast age, water warmth and room temperature; tight dough: rest before stretching; soggy centre: reduce wet toppings and preheat oven fully. Do not put unsupported raw dough directly on oven bars.

sources.title: KitchenAid AU: KSM195-linked manual, tool and speed charts pp. 5–6

note: Approx. 510 g dough. Source's relatively oil-rich formula retained. Research-based small-batch adaptation; not kitchen-tested. Do not taste raw dough or batter. Stop and unplug before tool changes; stop before scraping. KSM195 manual p. 5: mix and knead yeast dough at speed 2; do not use Stir/speed 1. Initial flex-edge mixing counts toward the heavy-run limit.

title: Sandwich bread (white tin loaf)
equipment: Mixer, flex-edge beater, dough hook, scales and approximately 21 × 11 × 7 cm loaf tin
time: 3–5½ hours, including two rises and full cooling; allow an extra 20-minute mixer rest if needed
intro: Start with the lower water quantity and add only enough to leave the dough lightly tacky.
steps: Check your exact model’s batch limit. Keep dough-hook kneading at speed 2. Count preliminary heavy mixing toward a maximum 5-minute heavy-mixing run, then rest the mixer 20 minutes before continuing, or follow a stricter model manual. Stop immediately if the mixer strains; hand-finish rather than increasing speed.

Fit the flex-edge beater in the 4.7 L bowl. Combine dry ingredients at speed 2 for 15 seconds. Add 250 ml water and oil; mix at speed 2 for 45–60 seconds, adding remaining water in 5–10 ml increments only if dry flour remains.

Stop and unplug to fit the hook. Knead at speed 2 for 2–3 minutes until smooth, springy and lightly tacky. If insufficiently developed, rest dough and mixer 20 minutes, then knead at speed 2 another 1–2 minutes, or finish by hand. Observe the model duty limit.
Cover in oiled bowl; prove 60–90 minutes until doubled. Deflate by hand; shape a tight log and put in greased tin.
Cover and prove 40–60 minutes until puffy and near the rim; a gentle finger dent should return slowly, not immediately.

Bake 200°C conventional / 180°C fan for 25–35 minutes until golden, loaf sides firm and base sounds hollow. Turn out; cool completely, about 1–2 hours, before slicing. Brush warm crust with a little oil if a softer crust is desired.
cue: Golden loaf with firm sides and a hollow-sounding base; cool fully before slicing.
troubleshoot: dense loaf: allow fuller rise, do not add excess flour; collapsed top: reduce final proof; gummy slices: bake longer and cool fully.

sources.title: KitchenAid AU: KSM195-linked manual, tool and speed charts pp. 5–6

note: Approximately 850–900 g dough. Adapted from the official white tin-loaf recipe; optional milk powder helps a softer sandwich crumb. Research-based small-batch adaptation; not kitchen-tested. Do not taste raw dough or batter. Stop and unplug before tool changes; stop before scraping. KSM195 manual p. 5: mix and knead yeast dough at speed 2; do not use Stir/speed 1. Initial flex-edge mixing counts toward the heavy-run limit.
yield: one approximately 21 × 11 × 7 cm loaf, 10–12 slices.

title: Rosemary focaccia
equipment: Mixer, flex-edge beater, dough hook, scales and approximately 20 × 30 cm metal tray
time: 2½–3¼ hours, including rest, two rises and baking
intro: Oiled hands preserve this dough’s softness better than extra flour when stretching it into the tray.
ingredients: olive oil 30 ml in dough + 20 ml for tin/top
steps: Check your exact model’s batch limit. Keep dough-hook kneading at speed 2. Count preliminary heavy mixing toward a maximum 5-minute heavy-mixing run, then rest the mixer 20 minutes before continuing, or follow a stricter model manual. Stop immediately if the mixer strains; hand-finish rather than increasing speed.
Fit the flex-edge beater in the 4.7 L bowl. Combine dry ingredients at speed 2 for 15 seconds; add water and 30 ml oil, then mix at speed 2 for 45 seconds until joined.
Hook at speed 2 for 2–3 minutes to a soft, stretchy dough; some sticking is normal. Cover and rest 20 minutes, then give one set of gentle stretch-and-folds by hand.
Cover in oiled bowl, prove about 60–90 minutes until doubled. Transfer to generously oiled tray; gently ease towards corners. Rest 10 minutes if resisting, then stretch again.
Cover 25–40 minutes until airy and puffy. Dimple with oiled fingers; distribute remaining oil, rosemary, garlic and flaky salt.
Bake 200°C conventional / 180°C fan for 25–30 minutes until golden top and cooked, golden underside. Cool 10 minutes on rack.
cue: Golden top and cooked, golden underside; airy dough before baking.
troubleshoot: sticky is expected; use oiled hands, not handfuls of extra flour. Tight stretching: rest. Pale wet base: use a metal tray and bake a little longer; shade exposed garlic if browning too quickly.

sources.title: KitchenAid AU: KSM195-linked manual, tool and speed charts pp. 5–6

note: Approximately 710 g dough, excluding topping. Editorial simpler, wetter, unfilled adaptation of the official herb-and-garlic recipe (Parmesan filling omitted). Research-based small-batch adaptation; not kitchen-tested. Do not taste raw dough or batter. Stop and unplug before tool changes; stop before scraping. KSM195 manual p. 5: mix and knead yeast dough at speed 2; do not use Stir/speed 1. Initial flex-edge mixing counts toward the heavy-run limit.
yield: one approximately 20 × 30 cm tray, 6 portions.

title: Brioche — overnight small loaf
equipment: Mixer, flex-edge beater, dough hook, scales and approximately 21 × 11 cm loaf tin
time: 13–17 hours or longer, including ≥8 hours chilling, proofing and cooling; 8–15 minutes active hook mixing in short runs plus 20-minute machine rests
intro: Cold overnight dough is easier to shape, while short speed-2 runs protect the mixer during enrichment.
ingredients: soft but not melting unsalted butter 115 g
additional beaten egg 15 g for glaze
steps: Check your exact model’s batch limit. Keep dough-hook kneading at speed 2. Count preliminary heavy mixing toward a maximum 5-minute heavy-mixing run, then rest the mixer 20 minutes before continuing, or follow a stricter model manual. Stop immediately if the mixer strains; hand-finish rather than increasing speed.

In a jug, stir milk, yeast and sugar together; wait 10 minutes if checking yeast activity. In the 4.7 L bowl, use the flex-edge beater at speed 2 to combine this with egg, flour and salt for 45–60 seconds, forming a shaggy dough. Rest covered 20 minutes.

Hook at speed 2 for 2 minutes. Add butter in three portions at 2, allowing roughly 1–2 minutes per portion until absorbed. Interrupt heavy mixing after at most 5 minutes including preliminary mixing, or sooner if the model manual requires; rest mixer 20 minutes before continuing. Keep dough covered; refrigerate it during breaks if warm or greasy.

Continue in 2–3-minute runs at 2, with required rests, until satiny and stretchy and a small piece stretches into a thin translucent membrane. Allow roughly 8–15 minutes total active hook time, not one continuous run. Hand-finish if necessary. Never use source's speed 4.
Cover, rise roughly 1–2 hours until doubled. Gently deflate/fold, cover and refrigerate at least 8 hours (overnight).
Divide cold dough into three equal balls or braid; place in buttered tin. Cover, prove approximately 2–3 hours until doubled/puffy; cold dough may take longer. Glaze lightly with egg.
Bake 170°C conventional / 150°C fan 25–35 minutes until deeply golden and centre set; extend baking if needed and tent top if darkening. Cool in tin 5–10 minutes, then rack completely.
cue: Satiny dough stretches into a thin translucent membrane; finished loaf is deeply golden with a set centre.
troubleshoot: greasy dough: butter/dough too warm; chill briefly. Dough tears: use rest and further gentle development, not higher speed. Slow final proof: wait for puffiness rather than baking to the clock.

sources.title: KitchenAid AU: KSM195-linked manual, tool and speed charts pp. 5–6

note: Approximately 577 g dough. Half-size source adaptation with shell-free egg weights. Research-based small-batch adaptation; not kitchen-tested. Do not taste raw dough or batter. Stop and unplug before tool changes; stop before scraping. KSM195 manual p. 5: mix and knead yeast dough at speed 2; do not use Stir/speed 1. title: Shortcrust pastry
equipment: Mixer, pastry beater, scales, rolling pin, wrap, 23 cm tart tin, baking paper and baking weights
time: 2–2½ hours, including ≥60 minutes chilling, 20–30 minutes lined-tin chilling and blind baking
intro: Visible pea-size butter pieces and minimal water help keep this pastry tender.
ingredients: optional caster sugar 10 g for sweet pastry
steps: Fit the supplied pastry beater in the 4.7 L bowl. Combine flour and salt/sugar at speed 2 for 10 seconds. Add cold butter and mix at speed 2 for about 30–60 seconds, only until coarse crumbs with some pea-size butter pieces remain. Watch the texture rather than insisting on a timer.
At speed 2, add water in small increments for about 10–20 seconds total, stopping when a squeezed handful holds together. Finish pressing together by hand; do not knead smooth.
Flatten to disc, wrap and chill at least 60 minutes. Roll 3 mm thick, line tin without stretching; chill another 20–30 minutes.

For an unfilled shell, line with baking paper and baking weights. Bake 200°C conventional / 180°C fan, 15–20 minutes; remove weights/paper and bake 8–12 minutes more until base dry and golden. For filled pies/tarts, follow filling recipe's baking instructions instead.
cue: Coarse crumbs before water; a squeezed handful holds together; baked shell has a dry golden base.
troubleshoot: crumbly: add water 5 ml at a time; sticky/greasy: chill, not more vigorous mixing; shrinkage: avoid stretching and allow chilling. Never use dough hook for this pastry.

note: Editorial classic 2:1 flour:butter shortcrust; source supports flat-beater technique, not this exact formula. Research-based small-batch adaptation; not kitchen-tested. KSM195 adaptation: use the supplied pastry beater, supported by its AU manual, rather than requiring a separate flat beater.

title: Chocolate chip cookies
equipment: Mixer, flex-edge beater, scales, lined baking trays and cooling rack
time: 35–65 minutes, including optional 20–30 minutes chilling and tray cooling
intro: Weigh the beaten egg and yolk separately for a practical small batch without guessing half an egg.
steps: Combine butter/sugars on 2 30 seconds, then 4 for 2–3 minutes until pale and creamy; stop and scrape midway.
Add egg/yolk and vanilla; 4 about 30–60 seconds until emulsified.
Add flour, bicarb and salt at Stir for 15–30 seconds, just until no flour streaks. Add chocolate at Stir 5–10 seconds or fold by hand.

Scoop 40 g portions; chill 20–30 minutes if soft. Place well apart on lined cool trays. Bake 180°C conventional / 160°C fan 11–14 minutes until edges golden and centres still soft but not liquid. Rest on trays 5 minutes then rack.
cue: Golden edges and soft but set centres, not liquid.
troubleshoot: excess spread: chill dough, use cool trays and weigh flour; tough: shorten flour mixing; crisp not chewy: remove earlier at set edges, allowing carry-over cooking.

title: Vanilla butter cake
equipment: Mixer, flex-edge beater, scales, 20 cm round tin and cooling rack
time: 1½–2 hours, including baking and full cooling
intro: Room-temperature butter, eggs and milk help this small cake batter emulsify evenly.
steps: Grease and line a 20 cm round tin. Heat oven 175°C conventional / 155°C fan. Combine butter/sugar 2 30–60 seconds; increase to 4–6 for 3–4 minutes until pale and fluffy, stopping to scrape.
Add egg gradually on 4, about 1 minute total, then vanilla. Scrape.
Sift flour, baking powder and salt. At Stir/2, alternate dry ingredients and milk in three additions; mix only until combined, roughly 30–60 seconds total. Hand-fold any flour pockets.
Scrape into tin; bake 30–40 minutes until centre springs back and skewer has no wet batter. Cool in tin 10–15 minutes, then rack completely.
cue: Centre springs back and a skewer has no wet batter.
troubleshoot: curdling: match egg/milk/butter temperatures; a little measured flour from the recipe can help. Dense cake: cream thoroughly but do not overmix flour. Brown top/wet middle: tent loosely and continue baking, checking oven temperature.

note: Approximately 775 g batter. Small-batch editorial adaptation: source's combined baking-powder/bicarb text is malformed and includes bicarb without an obvious acidic ingredient; this draft deliberately uses 4 g baking powder only rather than silently reproducing that ambiguity. The changed formula must be kitchen-validated before describing as tested. Research-based small-batch adaptation; not kitchen-tested. Do not taste raw dough or batter. title: Pancake batter
equipment: Mixer, flex-edge beater, measuring jug, frying pan and stove
time: 30–45 minutes, including 10–20 minutes batter rest
intro: Small lumps are welcome: stop mixing before the batter becomes completely smooth.
steps: flex-edge beater, Stir dry ingredients 10–15 seconds. Precombine milk, egg, oil and vanilla in a jug.
Add liquids on Stir/2, 15–25 seconds only until no dry flour streaks; some small lumps should remain. Stop rather than beating smooth. Rest 10–20 minutes while heating pan.

Lightly grease pan on medium heat. Ladle about 60 ml batter per pancake. Cook 2–3 minutes until bubbles form and edges look set; flip once and cook 1–2 minutes more until golden underneath and centre cooked. Do not press flat.
cue: Bubbles and set edges before flipping; golden underside and cooked centre afterward.
troubleshoot: rubbery: overmixed or pressed after flipping; burnt outside/raw centre: lower heat; too thick after resting: stir in 5–10 ml extra milk by hand.

sources.title: KitchenAid: how to make homemade pancakes
KitchenAid AU: KSM195-linked manual, tool and speed charts pp. 5–6

note: Editorial small-batch formulation based on official ingredient list and mixer method; source does not provide quantities. Research-based small-batch adaptation; not kitchen-tested. Do not taste raw dough or batter. Stop and unplug before tool changes; stop before scraping.
yield: approximately 8 pancakes using 60 ml batter each, 3–4 portions.

title: Basic crêpe batter
equipment: KSM195, supplied flex-edge beater, jug, sieve, ladle, approximately 20 cm non-stick frying pan and thin spatula
yield: Around 12 thin crêpes, depending on pan size and batter per crêpe
time: About 10 minutes preparation, 30 minutes refrigerated resting and 15–20 minutes cooking
intro: One thin, unsweetened batter for lemon and sugar, chocolate, or savoury fillings. No baking powder.
ingredients: 25 g unsalted butter, melted and cooled slightly
A little extra butter for the pan
steps: In a jug, lightly beat eggs with milk and water. Fit the flex-edge beater in the 4.7 L bowl while the mixer is off and unplugged. Add sifted flour and salt; lower and lock the head.

On Stir, gradually pour in the liquid mixture, then use speed 2 briefly, about 30–60 seconds, just until smooth. Stop and scrape only while stopped. If small lumps remain, pass the batter through a sieve rather than beating it for several minutes. Do not use high-speed creaming or whipping.

Cover and refrigerate the batter for 30 minutes. Add the slightly cooled melted butter and combine at Stir for 5–10 seconds, or stir by hand. The batter should pour like thin cream; if too thick to swirl, add water 5–10 ml at a time.

Heat the pan over medium heat and very lightly grease with butter. For a roughly 20 cm pan, start with about 35–45 ml batter, immediately tilting and swirling to coat the base in a thin layer. Adjust the next crêpe to the pan.

Cook about 45–60 seconds until the surface is set and the underside lightly golden. Loosen the edge and flip; cook another 20–30 seconds until lightly freckled with no wet batter remaining. Adjust heat if it colours before setting.

Serve as you go, or stack with baking paper between crêpes. Add sweet or savoury fillings after cooking. Keep unused batter refrigerated at 4°C or below and use within 24 hours; do not taste raw batter.
cue: Thin, pourable batter; cooked crêpes are flexible and lightly freckled, not thick or fluffy.
troubleshoot: Rubbery: batter was overworked or crêpes overcooked. Thick: use less batter or thin with a little water. Sticking: let the pan warm properly, grease lightly and wait until the first side sets before flipping. The first crêpe is a useful test of pan heat and batter quantity.

sources.title: KitchenAid AU: KSM195-linked mixing and tool guide

note: Source-informed KSM195 adaptation, not kitchen-tested by us. Ingredient formula follows Good Food’s classic crêpes, including the 100 ml water specified in its method. Flex-edge mixing speeds/times, refrigerated rest and pan-volume guidance are editorial adaptations of its hand-whisk method. Use plain flour, not self-raising flour. No sugar is needed in the base, so it works for sweet and savoury fillings. Contains wheat, milk and eggs.

title: Vanilla buttercream
equipment: Mixer, flex-edge beater, scales, sieve and spatula
time: 15–20 minutes; cake must already be completely cool
intro: Hold some cream back so the buttercream stays spreadable rather than runny.
steps: Beat butter 2 30 seconds, then 4–6 2–3 minutes until creamy and paler. Stop and scrape.
Add icing sugar in three portions on Stir, roughly 30 seconds each until contained, then 4 2–3 minutes until light.
Add vanilla, salt and cream gradually at 2, about 30 seconds; hold back liquid once spreadable. Beat 4 1 minute, then 2 1–2 minutes to reduce large air bubbles. Use only on fully cooled cake.
cue: Light, smooth, spreadable frosting without large air bubbles.
troubleshoot: gritty: sift and use pure icing sugar; too loose: chill briefly, then beat at low speed; too firm: add cream 5 ml at a time; bubbles: final slow paddle mixing. Contains dairy: refrigerate covered and soften gently before rebeating.

sources.title: KitchenAid AU: KSM195-linked manual, tool and speed charts pp. 5–6

note: Source uses vanilla beans and 3 tablespoons cream; metric draft deliberately uses extract and a restrained 40 ml cream, adding to texture rather than converting ambiguous tablespoon conventions. Research-based small-batch adaptation; not kitchen-tested. Do not taste raw dough or batter. Stop and unplug before tool changes; stop before scraping.
yield: approximately 540 g, enough for 12 generously iced cupcakes or a modest coating on one 20 cm cake.

title: Baked meringues
equipment: Mixer, wire whisk, grease-free bowl, scales and lined trays
time: 2¾–4 hours, including 75–100 minutes baking and 1–2 hours oven cooling
intro: Dissolve the sugar before piping for glossy meringues that dry without weeping.
steps: Bowl and whisk must be scrupulously clean and grease-free. Whisk whites starting 2, then 6 for 1–3 minutes until soft peaks (tips droop).

Add sugar gradually, about 15 g every 15–20 seconds on 6–8, allowing roughly 4–6 minutes; whisk another 1–2 minutes if needed until stiff, glossy peaks and sugar feels dissolved when a little mixture is rubbed between clean fingers. Do not keep whipping once dry or clumpy.
Mix cornflour, vinegar and vanilla at Stir 5–10 seconds. Pipe/spoon 16 mounds onto lined trays.

Bake 110°C conventional / 90°C fan for about 75–100 minutes until dry to touch and releasing easily from paper; time depends on size. Turn off oven and cool inside, door slightly ajar, about 1–2 hours. Store fully cooled in airtight container. This is a baked sweet, not raw topping.
cue: Stiff glossy peaks with dissolved sugar; baked meringues are dry and release from paper.
troubleshoot: whites will not whip: any yolk/fat contamination means restart with clean equipment; gritty/weeping: add sugar more slowly and dissolve fully; cracks: lower oven temperature and cool slowly; sticky after cooling: humidity or insufficient drying, dry further in low oven.

sources.title: KitchenAid AU: KSM195-linked manual, tool and speed charts pp. 5–6

note: Editorial all-caster-sugar adaptation at 2:1 sugar:white ratio; source uses mixed brown/caster sugar and a shorter, hotter bake. Research-based small-batch adaptation; not kitchen-tested. Do not taste raw dough or batter. Stop and unplug before tool changes; stop before scraping.
yield: approximately 16 small meringues.
bowl: 2.8 L stainless steel bowl with wire whisk; 4.7 L bowl also available

title: Egg pasta & tagliatelle
equipment: mixer bowl, dough hook; compatible KitchenAid pasta roller; scales, wrap/container, bench scraper, sharp knife and board, dusted tray/rack, large saucepan. Fettuccine cutter is optional, but produces 6.5 mm fettuccine, not an attachment expressly named tagliatelle.
time: 1–1½ hours, including 30-minute dough rest, rolling and cooking
intro: A weighed egg-to-flour ratio makes consistent sheets and wider hand-cut tagliatelle.
ingredients: 300 g plain/all-purpose flour or pasta-grade tipo 00
150 g beaten whole egg without shells (about 3 medium-to-large eggs, weigh rather than assume)
15–25 g additional flour for dusting (not automatically mixed into dough)
steps: Stop and unplug before tool or attachment changes. Dough-hook kneading and the documented pasta roller both use mixer speed 2, not the thickness dial. Count preliminary heavy mixing toward a maximum 5-minute heavy-mixing run, then rest the mixer 20 minutes before continuing, or use a stricter manual limit. Hand-finish if the motor strains.

In the 4.7 L bowl, mix flour and optional salt with the weighed egg by hand using a fork or spatula, until squeezed crumbs hold together. Add water 2–5 g at a time only if needed. The supplied flex-edge beater is not required for these stiff crumbs.

Stop, fit the dough hook, knead speed 2 for about 2 minutes. A stiff pasta dough may not form a perfect mixer ball. Gather and finish by hand briefly if necessary rather than running a struggling motor longer. Aim for firm, pliable dough, not wet/sticky bread dough.
Wrap and rest 30 minutes at cool room temperature. Keep unused quarters covered. Divide into four pieces; flatten each by hand.

Roller at mixer speed 2, thickness dial 1: pass, fold in half and pass again about 3 times, until smooth and cohesive. Dust very lightly. Then pass progressively at dials 2, 3, 4, 5, without folding. Dial 4–5 is the official sheet/fettuccine range. Use 5 for this starting recipe; thickness and tenderness are the cues, not a universal millimetre claim.

Sheets: cut to pan size, keep covered until cooking or filling. Tagliatelle: let sheets become touch-dry 5–10 minutes, still flexible, dust, loosely fold and cut by hand into 7–8 mm ribbons, then uncoil. Alternative: fit the 6.5 mm fettuccine cutter while unplugged and run at speed 5; label result fettuccine.

Boil ribbons in generously salted water; check after 60–90 seconds, usually 2–4 minutes depending on thickness. Bite should be tender with a slight resistance, not a raw floury core. Sheets used in lasagne need a separate assembly/baking recipe; do not imply the sheet-making card is a complete safe baked dish.

Never taste uncooked flour or dough. Keep egg dough and ricotta at 4°C or below when holding; refrigerate promptly and use by the next day or freeze. Let roller debris dry about 1 hour and brush out; never immerse, dishwash, run a cloth through rollers or scrape with a knife.
cue: Firm pliable dough, smooth flexible sheets; cooked ribbons have slight resistance but no raw floury core.
troubleshoot: cracks or tearing: hydrate sparingly and rest, avoid jumping thin settings; shrinking: cover and rest another 10 minutes; sticking: dust lightly and let surface dry briefly; cutters fail to separate: sheets too wet or too thick, allow touch-drying. Do not keep adding flour until dough is brittle. Refrigerate promptly or freeze dusted nests individually before bagging.

sources.title: KitchenAid perfect dough and speed 2 paddle
KitchenAid AU: KSM195-linked manual, tool and speed charts pp. 5–6

note: editorial home-batch formulation using the classic approximately 100 g flour : 50 g whole egg ratio, with official KitchenAid mixing/rolling technique. Not an exact reproduction of its manual's larger flour-measured recipe. Research-based draft; not kitchen-tested. Elapsed times and yields are estimates; use texture endpoints. Keep perishables at 4°C or below and cumulative room-temperature handling under 2 hours, or 1 hour above 32°C. KSM195 adaptation: stiff pasta crumbs are initially combined by hand, then briefly worked with the supplied dough hook; no separate flat beater is assumed.
yield: about 450–465 g dough; 3 generous or 4 moderate main-course portions; sheets or ribbons as required.

title: Egg-free semolina pasta
equipment: bowl, dough hook, scraper, board; optional roller and knife; pot/tray.
time: 1–1½ hours, including 30–45 minutes dough rest and hand shaping
intro: Finely remilled durum semolina hydrates into firm, egg-free dough suited especially to hand shapes.
ingredients: 300 g fine semola rimacinata di grano duro (finely remilled durum semolina, not coarse semolina pudding grains)
steps: Stop and unplug before tool or attachment changes. Dough-hook kneading and the documented pasta roller both use mixer speed 2, not the thickness dial. Count preliminary heavy mixing toward a maximum 5-minute heavy-mixing run, then rest the mixer 20 minutes before continuing, or use a stricter manual limit. Hand-finish if the motor strains.

In the 4.7 L bowl, combine fine semolina and warm water by hand using a fork or spatula until cohesive crumbs form. Fit the dough hook and work at speed 2 for about 2 minutes; hand-finish until smooth, roughly 5–8 more minutes as needed, rather than forcing a struggling mixer.

Cover and rest 30–45 minutes to hydrate fully. Shape small cavatelli or orecchiette by hand, or divide into quarters and roll with the optional roller at mixer speed 2: start thickness dial 1, fold until smooth, then narrow progressively to 4–5. Hand-cut ribbons. Cook in salted boiling water, checking from 2–3 minutes; thick hand shapes may take 4–6 minutes or longer. Cook until no hard or raw centre remains.

Never taste raw flour or dough. Refrigerate promptly when holding and use by the next day or freeze. If using a roller, let dough debris dry about 1 hour and brush out; never immerse, dishwash, run a cloth through rollers or scrape with a knife.
cue: Firm dough becomes supple after resting; cooked shapes have no hard or raw centre.
troubleshoot: dough feels relatively firm at first and becomes supple with rest. Sandy cracking: use finer flour, longer covered rest, or knead with wet hands; do not pour in large extra quantities of water. Sticky: tiny dusting of semolina. If it resists rolling, use hand shapes or rest longer rather than forcing it. Egg-free is still wheat-containing and raw flour is still unsafe to taste.

sources.title: KitchenAid AU: KSM195-linked manual, tool and speed charts pp. 5–6

note: ¾ of pasta specialist Gabriella Simonian's 400 g flour / 200 ml water recipe; mixer-assisted initial mixing is editorial and follows KitchenAid's conservative pasta sequence rather than the source's hand kneading. Research-based draft; not kitchen-tested. Elapsed times and yields are estimates; use texture endpoints. Keep perishables at 4°C or below and cumulative room-temperature handling under 2 hours, or 1 hour above 32°C. KSM195 adaptation: stiff pasta crumbs are initially combined by hand, then briefly worked with the supplied dough hook; no separate flat beater is assumed.
yield: about 450 g dough, 3–4 portions. Best suited to hand shapes; roller ribbons are an option, not a promise that every coarse semolina flour will roll well.

title: Ricotta ravioli
equipment: mixer/pasta roller; bowl, teaspoon or piping bag, pastry brush, pasta wheel/knife, dusted tray; no ravioli-making attachment required.
time: 1½–2 hours from raw dough, including dough rest, rolling, filling and cooking
intro: Drained ricotta and air-free seams matter more than a specialist ravioli-making attachment.
ingredients: 450 g egg pasta dough: 300 g plain or tipo 00 flour, 150 g beaten whole egg, 0–15 g water as needed, optional 1 g salt; 15–25 g extra flour for dusting
finely grated zest of ½ lemon
up to 1 g salt, adjusted for cheese
steps: Stop and unplug before tool or attachment changes. Dough-hook kneading and the documented pasta roller both use mixer speed 2, not the thickness dial. Count preliminary heavy mixing toward a maximum 5-minute heavy-mixing run, then rest the mixer 20 minutes before continuing, or use a stricter manual limit. Hand-finish if the motor strains.

Prepare 450 g egg pasta dough: mix 300 g plain or tipo 00 flour with 150 g weighed beaten egg using the flex-edge beater at speed 2 for about 30 seconds. If crumbs will not cohere, add water 2–5 g at a time, up to 15 g. Hook at speed 2 for about 2 minutes, hand-finish briefly, wrap and rest 30 minutes. Reserve 15–25 g extra flour for light dusting; optional 1 g salt belongs in the dough.

Divide dough into four pieces and keep waiting pieces covered. Flatten one piece by hand. With mixer at speed 2 and roller thickness dial 1, pass, fold and repeat about three times until smooth. Narrow progressively through dials 2, 3, 4 and 5 without further folding; use only light dusting. Then fill and seal by hand.

keep ricotta cold; drain until it holds a mound without weeping. Mix filling by hand. Roll dough as described above to thickness dial 5, within the official KitchenAid ravioli range. Fill one workable sheet at a time, keeping the others covered. Place about 7–9 g filling per raviolo, leaving at least 1 cm sealing margin. Lightly dampen bare margins only if necessary. Cover with another sheet or fold; press out air from around each mound, then press margins firmly and cut. Do not flour sealing surfaces heavily. Cook promptly in gently boiling salted water about 3–4 minutes, checking a piece: pasta edges should be tender and filling hot. Floating alone is not proof of doneness. Refrigerate overnight at most or freeze on a tray until solid (about 1–2 hours) then bag; cook from frozen, allowing extra time and checking centre rather than promising a fixed number.

Never taste uncooked flour or dough. Keep egg dough and ricotta at 4°C or below when holding; refrigerate promptly and use by the next day or freeze. Let roller debris dry about 1 hour and brush out; never immerse, dishwash, run a cloth through rollers or scrape with a knife.
cue: Seams are firmly sealed with no trapped air; cooked edges are tender and the filling hot.
troubleshoot: bursts: trapped air, excess filling or vigorous boil; leaking seams: flour on seal, dried sheets or over-wetting; watery centre: insufficiently drained ricotta. Keep filling cold while rolling, do not leave assembled trays out all afternoon. A raw meat filling would need a separate validated safe-cooking method and is not covered here.

title: Quick vanilla — churn and eat
bowl: Optional 5KSMICM freeze bowl, completely frozen before use
equipment: KSM195, compatible pre-frozen 5KSMICM bowl, its dasher and drive, measuring jug and spoon; no wire whisk for churning
yield: Approximately 800 ml–1 L soft ice cream, about 6 small servings; aeration varies
time: About 5 minutes mixing + 20–30 minutes churning, once the bowl is fully frozen; no freezer-hardening wait for soft-serve
intro: Four ingredients, no eggs, no cooking. Churn a cold base and eat it straight from the bowl as soft-serve.
ingredients: 400 ml refrigerator-cold pasteurized whipping cream (about 35% fat)
steps: Freeze the attachment bowl fully beforehand. The AU 5KSMICM page specifies 16 hours minimum; plan at least 24 hours and follow your exact manual. A bowl merely chilled in the refrigerator will not freeze ice cream. Keep it in the freezer until the base is ready.

In a jug, stir the cold milk and caster sugar for 1–2 minutes until the sugar dissolves. Gently stir in the cold cream and vanilla—do not whip them. Keep the base refrigerator-cold, ideally 4°C or below; if it warms during preparation, refrigerate until properly cold before proceeding. No extra overnight chilling is needed when the base is already cold.

With the mixer off and unplugged, fit the frozen bowl, correct dasher and drive assembly for the KSM195. Lower and lock the head. Start on Stir / the lowest speed BEFORE slowly pouring in the cold base. The approximately 700 ml starting base is below the documented 1.4 L starting-liquid limit.

Churn on Stir for about 20–30 minutes, checking the texture. Stop when thick, spoonable and holding soft ridges, like soft-serve. Do not increase speed or keep churning to force firm scoops; stop immediately if the dasher stalls.

Serve straight away in chilled bowls or cones. This is ready to eat but softer than tub ice cream. Only if you want firmer scoops, transfer to a covered freezer-safe container and freeze 2–4 hours. Freeze any leftovers promptly; fully refreeze the attachment bowl before another batch.
cue: Thick, spoonable soft-serve with ridges left by the dasher—not firm supermarket-style scoops.
troubleshoot: Still liquid: the bowl was not completely frozen, the base was too warm, the batch too large or assembly incorrect. Stop and refrigerate the base; fully refreeze the bowl before retrying. Butter flecks or a greasy texture: overchurning; stop as soon as soft-serve is ready. Do not reduce the sugar casually—it affects freezing, not only sweetness.

title: The most basic vanilla ice cream
equipment: KSM195, supplied wire whisk, refrigerator, spatula and covered freezer-safe container; no ice-cream attachment
bowl: 4.7 L stainless steel bowl with wire whisk
yield: Approximately 1.2–1.5 L, about 8 servings; yield depends on aeration
time: About 5–10 minutes preparation, then at least 6 hours freezing; overnight is easiest
intro: Three ingredients. Whisk, freeze, scoop. No eggs, cooking or special attachment.
ingredients: 600 ml cold pasteurized pure or thickened whipping cream (about 35% fat; not light cream)
395 g sweetened condensed milk (one standard Australian can; not evaporated milk)
10 ml vanilla extract or vanilla bean paste
steps: Fit the wire whisk in the 4.7 L bowl while the mixer is off and unplugged. Use refrigerator-cold cream and preferably chilled condensed milk. Add cream, condensed milk and vanilla; lower and lock the head.

Start at speed 2 to combine, then gradually increase to 6–8. Whisk until thick and airy with soft peaks that gently droop—usually a few minutes. Watch continuously and stop before it becomes grainy or separates; do not chase a fixed mixing time.

Scrape into a shallow freezer-safe container, cover and freeze at −18°C or colder for at least 6 hours, preferably overnight, until firm through the centre. Do not freeze it in the mixer bowl if you need that bowl for another job.
Let stand briefly, about 5–10 minutes, before scooping. Return the container to the freezer promptly; avoid repeated thawing and refreezing. Hand-wash the KSM195 wire whisk.
cue: Thick, airy soft peaks before freezing; firm through the centre after freezing.
troubleshoot: If it will not whip, check that the cream is cold and full-fat whipping cream, not light or cooking cream. If grainy, stop: it is overwhipped. If hard straight from the freezer, allow a few minutes to soften. Condensed milk supplies the sugar as well as milk solids; evaporated milk is not a substitute.

title: Vanilla custard ice cream
equipment: Compatible mixer and pre-frozen ice-cream bowl, correct dasher and drive, scales, measuring jug, silicone spatula and covered shallow freezer container; saucepan, whisk, fine sieve, thermometer and ice-water bath
time: 7–10 hours after bowl is frozen, including ≥4 hours base chilling and 2–4 hours hardening; freeze bowl ≥24 hours ahead
intro: A thermometer takes the guesswork out of safely thickening this egg custard.
ingredients: 400 ml pure or thickened whipping cream, about 35% fat
5 ml vanilla extract (or ½ split vanilla pod plus a little extract)
steps: Freeze the compatible ice-cream bowl for at least 24 hours; follow the exact attachment manual if it requires longer. Use pasteurized dairy where specified.
heat milk, sugar and salt until steaming and dissolved.
If using pod, scrape seeds in, cover off heat and infuse 30–60 minutes, then rewarm.
Whisk yolks in a bowl; gradually whisk in a little warm milk, then return to saucepan.
Stir/scrape continuously on gentle heat to 77–82°C, until custard coats the spatula and a finger-drawn line stays clear; do not boil.
Strain immediately into the cream, stir in vanilla and cool in an ice bath.
Refrigerate at least 4 hours, preferably overnight until ≤4°C.
Remove pod.
Chill the base to 4°C or below. Measure its cooled volume: the maximum starting base is 1.4 L, not the 1.9 L finished capacity. Do not double this batch blindly.

Stop and unplug to fit the frozen bowl, correct dasher and drive. Start the dasher on Stir / lowest speed before pouring in the cold base; never pour into a stationary dasher. Churn about 20–30 minutes until thick soft-serve with tracks and ridges. Stop immediately if the dasher stalls; do not increase speed.

Pack into a cold covered shallow container and freeze at −18°C or colder 2–4 hours until scoopable. Completely refreeze the bowl before another batch; allow it to reach room temperature before hand-washing and follow its generation-specific cleaning instructions.
cue: Custard reaches 77–82°C and coats a spatula with a clear drawn line; churned ice cream forms thick soft-serve ridges.
troubleshoot: scrambled flecks mean overheating; immediate fine straining may help small flecks but a severely curdled/scorched batch will not become smooth ice cream. Do not use a spoon-coating cue as a replacement for thermometer safety. Icy: insufficiently frozen bowl/warm base or reduced sugar/fat; butter flecks: overchurning very fatty cream. Use pasteurized dairy and preferably yolks. If the base stays liquid after 20–30 minutes, stop and refrigerate it; check bowl freeze, base temperature, assembly and volume before retrying with a fully refrozen bowl. Never solve a stalled dasher with more speed or hot water.

title: No-egg chocolate ice cream
equipment: Compatible mixer and pre-frozen ice-cream bowl, correct dasher and drive, scales, measuring jug, silicone spatula and covered shallow freezer container; saucepan, whisk, fine sieve, thermometer and ice-water bath

intro: Cooked starch and melted chocolate give this egg-free ice cream its dense texture.
steps: Freeze the compatible ice-cream bowl for at least 24 hours; follow the exact attachment manual if it requires longer. Use pasteurized dairy where specified.
whisk cocoa, sugar, starch and salt in saucepan.
Gradually whisk in cold water and milk until smooth.
Heat with frequent stirring, then near-constant stirring as hot, until the mixture comes to a boil and thickens.
Remove from heat, add chocolate and stir until glossy and fully melted; add vanilla.
Cool promptly in an ice bath, cover and chill 4 hours or overnight.
Stir the cold thick base smooth and verify volume.
Chill the base to 4°C or below. Measure its cooled volume: the maximum starting base is 1.4 L, not the 1.9 L finished capacity. Do not double this batch blindly.

Stop and unplug to fit the frozen bowl, correct dasher and drive. Start the dasher on Stir / lowest speed before pouring in the cold base; never pour into a stationary dasher. Use pasteurized milk; check chocolate allergens. Cornstarch is not instant ClearJel and must be cooked. If the base stays liquid after 20–30 minutes, stop and refrigerate it; check bowl freeze, base temperature, assembly and volume before retrying with a fully refrozen bowl. 225 ml freshly squeezed lemon juice, strained
finely grated yellow zest of 2–3 washed unwaxed lemons (no white pith). No alcohol or raw egg

Add zest and lemon juice; cool promptly.
Refrigerate at least 2 hours, longer until ≤4°C.
Add remaining 100 ml cold water; sieve if a smooth zest-free texture is wanted.
Chill the base to 4°C or below. Measure its cooled volume: the maximum starting base is 1.4 L, not the 1.9 L finished capacity. Do not double this batch blindly.

Stop and unplug to fit the frozen bowl, correct dasher and drive. Start the dasher on Stir / lowest speed before pouring in the cold base; never pour into a stationary dasher. Churn about 20–30 minutes until thick soft-serve with tracks and ridges. Stop immediately if the dasher stalls; do not increase speed.

title: Pistachio gelato-style ice cream

steps: Freeze the compatible ice-cream bowl for at least 24 hours; follow the exact attachment manual if it requires longer. Use pasteurized dairy where specified.
whisk starch into 60 ml of the milk until smooth.
Heat remaining milk with sugar until almost boiling.
Whisk in slurry and gently simmer 3 minutes, stirring continuously; it should lightly thicken, not scorch.
Transfer to bowl, cool promptly in an ice bath, cover and refrigerate 4 hours or preferably overnight.
Whisk in pistachio cream and optional citrus until completely smooth and evenly coloured; keep ≤4°C (re-chill if necessary).

Stop and unplug to fit the frozen bowl, correct dasher and drive. Start the dasher on Stir / lowest speed before pouring in the cold base; never pour into a stationary dasher. Pack into a cold covered shallow container and freeze at −18°C or colder 2–4 hours until scoopable. Completely refreeze the bowl before another batch; allow it to reach room temperature before hand-washing and follow its generation-specific cleaning instructions.

troubleshoot: gritty: nut product not finely ground or cream not dispersed; use smooth purchased cream rather than chopped nuts. Hard/bland: wrong product, especially substituting pure unsweetened paste without rebalancing sugar/fat. Sweetened spreads vary significantly; recipe needs practical testing with the selected brand. No validated one-for-one conversion to pure paste is supplied. Nut + milk allergens; inspect spread label for soy/other nuts. Natural colour is usually muted green/beige, not fluorescent green. title: Whipped cream
equipment: Mixer, wire whisk, bowl, refrigerator and spatula

intro: Cold cream and chilled tools help you reach soft peaks before the cream starts separating.

steps: Chill bowl and whisk for about 10 minutes. Add cold cream, icing sugar and vanilla.

title: Homemade butter
equipment: Mixer, wire whisk, flex-edge beater, bowl, sieve or cheesecloth, spatula and ice-cold water
time: 20–30 minutes, including whipping, draining and washing
intro: Washing away the trapped sweet-cream liquid gives the butter a cleaner texture and flavour.
ingredients: 500 ml pasteurized pure or thickened whipping cream (about 35% fat)
Ice-cold water, about 60 ml per wash, repeated as needed
steps: Add cream to bowl. Start low and gradually increase to a whipping speed, using a compatible shield if needed. Whip past cream peaks until yellow butter solids separate from liquid, around 10 minutes but variable.
Stop and drain liquid through a sieve or cheesecloth; press solids gently.

Wash the drained butter by hand in a clean bowl: add about 60 ml ice-cold water, press gently with a spatula, drain cloudy water and repeat until water stays clear. Press out water; do not force the wire whisk through firm butter.
Stop and unplug to fit the flex-edge beater. Add optional salt and mix briefly on low just until combined. Wrap and refrigerate at 4°C or below.
cue: Distinct yellow butter solids separate from liquid; final wash water stays clear.
troubleshoot: If separation is slow, continue watching rather than assuming a fixed whipping time. Cloudy washing water means more liquid remains trapped; wash again and press out water. Stop before draining or scraping and do not let the machine strain against firm butter.

title: Mashed potatoes
equipment: Mixer, pastry beater, bowl, scales, saucepan, stove and colander

intro: Add warm milk gradually and stop early to avoid turning the potatoes gluey.
steps: Cut potatoes into even pieces, cover with water in a saucepan, bring to a boil and simmer until completely tender, about 15–25 minutes depending on size. The mixer does not cook them.
Drain thoroughly, allow steam to escape briefly and warm the milk separately.
Fit pastry beater. Put hot cooked potatoes and butter into bowl, use speed 2, and gradually add 100 ml warm milk plus salt. Add up to 50 ml more milk only as needed.
Stop as soon as smooth or at your preferred texture; scrape only while stopped. Serve hot or cool promptly in shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 32°C.
cue: Tender potatoes crush easily; mash is soft with no hard pieces, not elastic or gluey.
troubleshoot: Hard lumps mean the potatoes were undercooked; cook them thoroughly before mixing. Excess milk makes loose mash, so hold some back. Gluey mash comes from overworking starch and cannot be fixed by further beating.

title: Shredded cooked chicken
equipment: Mixer, pastry beater, bowl, separate cooking appliance and food thermometer

Start briefly at speed 2, then use speed 4 for shredding as specified in the KSM195 manual. Check after 10–15 seconds and stop when shreds are the size you want; total time varies, so do not run for a fixed minute. Check texture while stopped. Add any sauce afterward to reduce splatter.
